transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?

Well, doctor, I suppose what brings me in is my eating. Once I start eating certain comfort foods, I tell myself, Maria, that is enough. But... my hand still goes right back to the pot. It is just like I can't make myself stop.
After these times when you feel unable to stop eating, do you do anything to try to compensate or get rid of the food, such as making yourself throw up?

No, doctor, I don't do anything like that. I... I never make myself throw up or anything. Once I eat it, it stays down. I just end up feeling overly full and upset with myself, but no, I don't try to get rid of the food.
On average, about how many times a week do these episodes where you feel unable to stop eating happen?

Well, since my friend passed away, it's been happening most weeks. I'd say usually once or twice a week. It mostly happens on those quiet afternoons, you know, after I get home from choir practice or when I'm done with my gardening.
During these times, would you say you eat an unusually large amount of food, much more than most people would eat in that amount of time?

Yes, I would say so. Like I mentioned about those afternoons after choir or working in the garden... I'll fix myself a plate of rice and beans, or maybe some chicken stew. And then I just keep going back to the pot for more. I don't stop until I've eaten enough for two or three whole meals. So, yes, it is definitely a lot more than most people would eat at one time.
About how many months has this pattern of overeating been going on?
Well, it started right after my close friend passed away. So... I'd say it has been going on for about three months now.
During these episodes, do you find yourself eating even when you don't feel physically hungry?
No, not really. I usually wait until I'm actually hungry before I start eating. It's just that once I start, I can't seem to stop.
During these times, do you find yourself eating much more rapidly than you normally would?

Yes, I do. I've always been a slow eater, normally. But lately, when this happens... I eat very fast. I'll just stand right there by the kitchen counter and eat, and I'm hardly even tasting the food before the next bite is already in my mouth.
During these episodes, do you tend to eat alone because you feel embarrassed by how much you are eating?
No, I don't really do that. I mean, I live alone anyway, so there's no one around to see me eat. I'm not hiding it from anybody, it's just just me in the house.
During these episodes, do you keep eating until you feel uncomfortably full?

Yes. By the time I finally stop, my stomach feels... well, it feels tight and heavy. I usually have to go sit down in my recliner and loosen my waistband, just because I went way past what actually felt comfortable.
After these episodes of overeating, do you often find yourself feeling disgusted with yourself, depressed, or very guilty?

Yes, I do. Afterward, I just feel... ashamed, and really sad. Cooking and eating used to be about family and caring for people, you know? Now it just feels like this awful thing I'm doing that I'd have to hide from the folks at my church. It makes me feel terrible about myself.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets diagnostic criteria for binge-eating disorder (classified under F50.8 in ICD-10). She reports recurrent binge eating episodes characterized by eating an objectively large amount of food (2-3 full meals) with a distinct sense of lack of control, occurring 1-2 times per week for the past 3 months. The episodes are accompanied by at least three associated features (eating much more rapidly than normal, eating until uncomfortably full, and experiencing intense guilt, shame, and sadness afterward). There are no compensatory behaviors such as purging, fasting, or excessive exercise, ruling out bulimia nervosa.
